question: How many countries share land boundaries with India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Seven.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India shares its land boundary with 7 countries — Bangladesh, China, Pakistan, Nepal, Myanmar, Bhutan and Afghanistan. (स्थल सीमा — land boundary)

• India's total land boundary is about 15,106.7 km, touching 17 Indian States/UTs.

• Longest land border: with Bangladesh (≈4,096.7 km); shortest: with Afghanistan (≈106 km).

• Sri Lanka and Maldives are neighbours by sea, not by land.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The border with China (≈3,488 km) is called the Line of Actual Control (LAC); with Pakistan it is the Line of Control (LoC) in J&K and the Radcliffe Line elsewhere.

• The Durand Line separates India (PoK region) and Pakistan from Afghanistan.

• West Bengal touches the highest number of countries (Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan).

NOTE

• Border-length order (descending): Bangladesh > China > Pakistan > Nepal > Myanmar > Bhutan > Afghanistan.

• Important boundary lines: McMahon Line (India–China, in Arunachal), Radcliffe Line (India–Pakistan/Bangladesh, 1947).

question: Indian musician Jagjit Singh is credited for the revival of _____ genre of music/poetry.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ghazal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Jagjit Singh (1941–2011), born at Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan, is popularly called the "Ghazal King" / Ghazal Samrat. (ग़ज़ल — a poetic form of couplets)

• He revived and popularised the ghazal in the 1970s–80s by simplifying its Urdu diction and blending it with light Indian and Western instrumentation, making it reach the common listener.

• His album "The Unforgettables" (1976), sung with his wife Chitra Singh, was a landmark ghazal record.

• He was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2003.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Latin and Jazz are Western music genres and have no link with Jagjit Singh.

• Sufi music in India is associated with names like Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, Abida Parveen and Wadali Brothers.

• Other great ghazal singers: Mehdi Hassan, Begum Akhtar, Ghulam Ali, Pankaj Udhas, Talat Aziz.

NOTE

• Jagjit Singh gave music for films such as Arth, Saath Saath, Prem Geet and for Gulzar's TV serial Mirza Ghalib.

• A commemorative postage stamp was released in his honour in 2014.

question: The Indian National Congress was established when 72 delegates from all over the country met at Bombay in December ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1885.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Indian National Congress (INC) was founded on 28 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, where 72 delegates from all over India assembled. (भारतीय राष्ट्रीय कांग्रेस)

• It was founded on the initiative of a retired British civil servant, A.O. Hume.

• Its first president was Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee (W.C. Bonnerjee).

• The first session was originally to be held at Poona, but was shifted to Bombay due to a cholera outbreak.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• 1858 — The Government of India Act, 1858 ended Company rule and transferred power to the British Crown.

• 1872 — Year of the first Census of India under Lord Mayo (the first synchronous census was 1881 under Lord Ripon).

• 1890 — Year in which Kadambini Ganguly became the first woman to address an INC session (Calcutta, 1890).

NOTE

• Dadabhai Naoroji was the first person to preside over the INC three times (1886, 1893, 1906).

• Annie Besant (1917, Calcutta) was the first woman president of INC; Sarojini Naidu (1925, Kanpur) was the first Indian woman president.

question: Which cell organelles help in intracellular digestion and are known as the "suicidal bags" of the cell?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lysosome.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing powerful hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes and carry out intracellular digestion of worn-out organelles and foreign particles. (लयनकाय)

• They are called the "suicidal bags" of the cell because when the cell is damaged or ageing, the lysosome membrane bursts and the enzymes digest the cell itself (autolysis).

• Lysosomes were discovered by Christian de Duve (Nobel Prize, 1974).

• They are formed by the Golgi apparatus and are absent in mature RBCs.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Golgi bodies — discovered by Camillo Golgi; act as the packaging, sorting and dispatching unit of the cell.

• Centrosome — contains centrioles; organises the spindle fibres during cell division (found in animal cells).

• Chloroplast — contains chlorophyll; site of photosynthesis; called the "kitchen of the cell".

NOTE

• Nicknames: Mitochondria — powerhouse of the cell; Ribosome — protein factory; Nucleus — brain/control room of the cell; Endoplasmic reticulum — transport channel.

• The term "cell" was coined by Robert Hooke (1665); cell theory was given by Schleiden and Schwann.

question: The "Double Dome" feature of Indo-Islamic architecture was introduced by which dynasty of Delhi Sultanate?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lodi Dynasty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The double dome (a dome with an outer shell and an inner shell) was introduced in Indian architecture on a full scale under the Lodi dynasty (1451–1526), the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. (दोहरा गुंबद)

• The Tomb of Sikandar Lodi (built 1517–18) in Delhi is regarded as the first true double dome structure in India.

• The device gave the monument an imposing outer height while keeping the interior proportionate; it was borrowed from Persian/Central Asian architecture.

• It was later perfected by the Mughals — as in Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Slave/Mamluk dynasty (1206–1290) — Qutub Minar (begun by Qutbuddin Aibak, completed by Iltutmish), Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra.

• Khilji dynasty (1290–1320) — Alai Darwaza (true arch and true dome), Siri Fort, Hauz Khas.

• Tughlaq dynasty (1320–1414) — Tughlaqabad Fort, Firoz Shah Kotla, city of Jahanpanah; noted for the batter (sloping walls) style.

NOTE

• The Lodi dynasty was founded by Bahlol Lodi (1451); its last ruler Ibrahim Lodi was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

• Lodi Gardens, Delhi houses the tombs of Sikandar Lodi and Mohammed Shah Sayyid.

question: "The Invisible Man" is a science fiction novel written by famous author ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Herbert George Wells.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "The Invisible Man" (1897) is a science fiction novel by the English writer H.G. Wells (Herbert George Wells, 1866–1946). (विज्ञान कथा — science fiction)

• It tells the story of Griffin, a scientist who makes himself invisible but cannot reverse the process.

• Wells is often called the "Father of Science Fiction", a title he shares with Jules Verne and Hugo Gernsback.

• Other famous works of Wells: The Time Machine (1895), The Island of Doctor Moreau (1896), The War of the Worlds (1898).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• William Shakespeare — English dramatist; wrote Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, King Lear, Romeo and Juliet; not a science fiction author.

• Jules Verne — French author of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, Around the World in Eighty Days, Journey to the Centre of the Earth.

• Agatha Christie — "Queen of Crime"; wrote Murder on the Orient Express, And Then There Were None; created detectives Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple.

NOTE

• H.G. Wells also wrote the non-fiction The Outline of History.

• Do not confuse this with Ralph Ellison's "Invisible Man" (1952), an American novel on racial identity.

question: Which of the following is "NOT" a biosphere reserve in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gir Forest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Gir Forest (Gujarat) is a National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary — the last natural home of the Asiatic lion — but it is NOT a notified Biosphere Reserve. (जीवमंडल आरक्षित क्षेत्र)

• India has 18 Biosphere Reserves, of which 12 are included in the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR).

• A biosphere reserve has three zones — core zone (fully protected), buffer zone and transition/manipulation zone.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Nilgiri (1986) — the first Biosphere Reserve of India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka).

• Sunderbans (1989) — West Bengal; largest mangrove area; famous for the Royal Bengal Tiger.

• Cold Desert (2009) — Himachal Pradesh; habitat of the snow leopard.

NOTE

• Other Biosphere Reserves: Nanda Devi, Nokrek, Great Nicobar, Gulf of Mannar, Manas, Simlipal, Pachmarhi, Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Khangchendzonga, Agasthyamala, Panna, Seshachalam, Kachchh (largest in area), Dibru-Saikhowa, Dehang-Debang.

• Project Lion was launched for the Asiatic lion of Gir; Project Tiger in 1973 and Project Elephant in 1992.

question: What was the purpose behind the Pillars of Ashoka?
solution_text:
The correct answer is To spread the dharma policies.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Pillars of Ashoka (Ashoka Stambha) carry inscriptions (Pillar Edicts) through which the Mauryan emperor Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE) propagated his policy of Dhamma — moral conduct, non-violence, tolerance, respect for elders and kindness to all beings. (धम्म — moral law)

• After the Kalinga War (261 BCE), Ashoka replaced bherighosha (the sound of the war drum) with dhammaghosha (the proclamation of dhamma).

• The edicts were written mainly in Prakrit using the Brahmi script (also Kharosthi, Greek and Aramaic in the north-west).

• Ashoka's Dhamma was not a new religion nor an instrument of forced conversion; it was a code of social ethics meant for all sects.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is wrong because Ashoka specifically gave up bherighosha after Kalinga.

• Options 2 and 3 are wrong because Ashoka's Dhamma preached religious tolerance, not mass conversion or sectarianism.

• The Lion Capital of Sarnath was adopted as the State Emblem of India on 26 January 1950.

NOTE

• Ashokan inscriptions were first deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837.

• The Dharma Chakra from the Sarnath capital appears at the centre of the Indian National Flag.

question: Which player was widely known by the name of Flying Sikh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Milkha Singh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Milkha Singh (1929–2021), the legendary Indian sprinter, was famously called the "Flying Sikh" — a title reportedly given by Pakistan's President Ayub Khan after Milkha beat Abdul Khaliq in Lahore. (उड़न सिख)

• He finished a heartbreaking fourth in the 400 m final at the 1960 Rome Olympics, setting a national record that stood for nearly 40 years.

• He won gold in the 1958 Commonwealth Games (Cardiff) — India's first individual athletics gold there — and golds at the 1958 and 1962 Asian Games.

• He was honoured with the Padma Shri in 1959; his autobiography is "The Race of My Life", which inspired the film Bhaag Milkha Bhaag (2013).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Harbhajan Singh — off-spinner, nicknamed "Turbanator"; first Indian to take a Test hat-trick (2001, vs Australia).

• Arshdeep Singh — left-arm fast bowler of the Indian cricket team.

• Yuvraj Singh — hit six sixes in an over off Stuart Broad (T20 World Cup 2007); Player of the Tournament, ICC World Cup 2011.

NOTE

• Other sporting nicknames: P.T. Usha — "Payyoli Express"/"Golden Girl"; Dhyan Chand — "The Wizard/Magician of Hockey"; Sachin Tendulkar — "Master Blaster".

question: Which of the following novels is written by Chetan Bhagat?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The 3 Mistakes of My Life.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "The 3 Mistakes of My Life" (2008) is a novel by the popular Indian English author Chetan Bhagat, set in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, against the backdrop of the 2001 earthquake and the 2002 Godhra riots.

• It was adapted into the Bollywood film "Kai Po Che!" (2013).

• Chetan Bhagat is an IIT Delhi and IIM Ahmedabad alumnus and a former investment banker.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• "The White Tiger" — written by Aravind Adiga; won the Man Booker Prize in 2008.

• "Untouchable" (1935) — a classic novel by Mulk Raj Anand on caste discrimination.

• "Our Story Needs No Filter" — written by Sudeep Nagarkar.

NOTE

• Other works of Chetan Bhagat: Five Point Someone (2004) → film *3 Idiots*; One Night @ the Call Center → *Hello*; 2 States ; Revolution 2020; Half Girlfriend; One Indian Girl; The Girl in Room 105; 400 Days.

• Indian Booker winners: Arundhati Roy — *The God of Small Things* (1997); Kiran Desai — *The Inheritance of Loss* (2006); Aravind Adiga — *The White Tiger* (2008).

question: Which among the following festivals is associated with Arunachal Pradesh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Solung.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Solung is a major agricultural festival of the Adi tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, celebrated in the first week of September (usually from 1 September) for about five days. (कृषि पर्व — harvest festival)

• It is celebrated after the sowing of seeds and prays for a rich harvest and the prosperity of humans and cattle.

• The Ponung dance performed by women is an important part of the Solung celebrations.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Wangala — the "Hundred Drums" harvest festival of the Garo tribe of Meghalaya, in honour of the sun god Saljong.

• Ugadi — the New Year festival of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka (called Gudi Padwa in Maharashtra).

• Pongal — the four-day harvest festival of Tamil Nadu, celebrated in the month of Thai (January).

NOTE

• Other festivals of Arunachal Pradesh: Losar (Monpa), Mopin (Galo), Nyokum (Nyishi), Dree (Apatani), Si-Donyi, Reh (Idu Mishmi).

• Arunachal Pradesh is known as the "Land of the Rising Sun" / "Land of the Dawn-lit Mountains"; capital Itanagar.

question: What is the capital of India's neighbouring country Afghanistan?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kabul.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan, situated on the Kabul River in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush mountains. (काबुल)

• The currency of Afghanistan is the Afghan Afghani; official languages are Pashto and Dari.

• Afghanistan shares a small land border with India (through the PoK region), making it one of India's 7 land neighbours.

• The Salma Dam (Afghan-India Friendship Dam) on the Hari Rud and the Afghan Parliament building were built with Indian assistance.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Karachi — the largest city and chief port of Pakistan; Pakistan's capital is Islamabad.

• Kathmandu — the capital of Nepal; currency Nepalese Rupee.

• Kandahar — the second-largest city of Afghanistan, not its capital.

NOTE

• Capitals of India's neighbours: Bangladesh — Dhaka; Bhutan — Thimphu; Myanmar — Nay Pyi Taw; China — Beijing; Sri Lanka — Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte (administrative); Maldives — Male.

• The Durand Line (1893) demarcates the Afghanistan–Pakistan boundary.

question: Respect for the National Flag and National Anthem is a ________ of every Indian citizen.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fundamental Duty.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 51A(a) makes it a Fundamental Duty of every citizen "to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem". (मौलिक कर्तव्य)

• Fundamental Duties are contained in Part IV-A of the Constitution and were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• Originally 10 duties were added; the 11th duty (providing education to children aged 6–14) was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

• Fundamental Duties were borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Rights — Part III (Articles 12–35), borrowed from the USA; justiciable.

• Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) — Part IV (Articles 36–51), borrowed from Ireland; non-justiciable.

• A legal right is created by ordinary law and is enforceable in ordinary courts, unlike a constitutional Fundamental Right.

NOTE

• Fundamental Duties, like DPSPs, are non-justiciable — they cannot be enforced by writs.

• The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 provides punishment for disrespecting the National Flag and Anthem.

question: Which of the following article of Indian constitution is related with "Promotion of International Peace and security"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 51.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 51 of the Indian Constitution deals with the "Promotion of International Peace and Security". It is a Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP) under Part IV. (अंतर्राष्ट्रीय शांति और सुरक्षा की अभिवृद्धि)

• It directs the State to (a) promote international peace and security, (b) maintain just and honourable relations between nations, (c) foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and (d) encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

• Do not confuse it with Article 51A, which lists the Fundamental Duties.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Article 40 — Organisation of Village Panchayats (a Gandhian principle).

• Article 43 — Living wage and decent conditions of work for workers, and promotion of cottage industries.

• Article 47 — Duty of the State to raise the level of nutrition and standard of living and to improve public health, including prohibition of intoxicating drinks and drugs.

NOTE

• Other important DPSPs: Article 39A — equal justice and free legal aid; Article 44 — Uniform Civil Code; Article 45 — early childhood care and education; Article 48A — protection of environment, forests and wildlife.

• DPSPs are non-justiciable (Article 37) but are "fundamental in the governance of the country".

question: In which type of farming the land is used for growing food and fodder crops and rearing livestock?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mixed farming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mixed farming is a system in which the same farm is used both for growing food and fodder crops and for rearing livestock (cattle, poultry, etc.). (मिश्रित कृषि)

• Crop residues feed the animals, and animal dung/manure fertilises the fields — making the system self-sustaining and less risky, since income comes from more than one source.

• It is common in the developed regions of Europe, eastern USA, Argentina, south-eastern Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Shifting cultivation ("slash and burn") — forest patches are cleared and burnt, cultivated for a few years and then abandoned; known as Jhum in the North-East, Podu in Andhra, Bewar/Penda in MP, Kumari in Kerala.

• Subsistence farming — the farmer grows food mainly for his own family's consumption, with little or no surplus for sale.

• Plantation agriculture — a single cash crop grown on a large estate, e.g. tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane, banana; capital and labour intensive.

NOTE

• Intensive farming uses a small area with high inputs and high yield; extensive farming uses large areas with machinery and lower per-hectare yield.

• Commercial farming is done mainly for sale in the market, using HYV seeds, fertilisers and irrigation.

question: Currency notes and coins are called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is fiat money.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Fiat money is money that has value because the government orders (Latin: fiat = "let it be done") that it shall be accepted as legal tender, and not because of any intrinsic worth of the material. (आदेशात्मक मुद्रा)

• Currency notes and coins in circulation in India are fiat money — they are backed by the guarantee of the Government of India / RBI, not by gold or silver of equal value.

• Fiat money is also legal tender, i.e. no one can legally refuse it in settlement of a debt.

• In India, currency notes (except the ₹1 note) are issued by the Reserve Bank of India, while coins and the ₹1 note are issued by the Ministry of Finance, Government of India.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Near money — highly liquid assets that are not money but can be quickly converted into cash, e.g. bonds, treasury bills, time deposits, bills of exchange.

• Commodity money — money whose value comes from the commodity itself, e.g. gold and silver coins.

• Fiduciary money — accepted on mutual trust between payer and payee and not backed by any government order, e.g. cheques and drafts.

NOTE

• The RBI issues currency under the Minimum Reserve System (since 1957) — it must keep a minimum reserve of ₹200 crore (₹115 crore in gold + ₹85 crore in foreign securities).

• Money supply measures: M1 (narrow money), M2, M3 (broad money) and M4.

question: The point on the surface, nearest to the focus of the earthquake, is called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is epicentre.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The point inside the earth where an earthquake originates is called the focus or hypocentre; the point on the earth's surface directly above the focus (and hence nearest to it) is the epicentre. (अधिकेंद्र)

• The epicentre experiences the earliest and the strongest tremors, and the intensity decreases as one moves away from it.

• Earthquake waves are recorded by a seismograph; magnitude is measured on the Richter scale and intensity on the Mercalli scale.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Hypocentre is another word for the focus — it lies below the surface, so it is not the surface point.

• Centrepiece and semi centre are not geographical/seismological terms.

• Seismic waves: P-waves (primary, longitudinal — travel through solids, liquids and gases; fastest), S-waves (secondary, transverse — travel only through solids) and L-waves (surface waves — most destructive).

NOTE

• The shadow zone of S-waves (beyond 103°) proves that the outer core of the earth is liquid.

• India is divided into four seismic zones (II, III, IV and V); Zone V is the most earthquake-prone.

question: Gangaur festival of Rajasthan is associated with which god and goddess?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Shiva and Goddess Parwati.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Gangaur is one of the most important festivals of Rajasthan, dedicated to Lord Shiva (Gan) and Goddess Parvati/Gauri (Gaur). The very name is formed from "Gan" + "Gaur". (गणगौर)

• It is celebrated in the month of Chaitra (March–April), beginning the day after Holi and continuing for 18 days, ending on Gangaur Teej (Chaitra Shukla Tritiya).

• Unmarried girls worship Gauri to get a good husband, while married women pray for the long life and well-being of their husbands.

• Clay images of Isar (Shiva) and Gauri (Parvati) are worshipped and then taken out in colourful processions, especially in Jaipur and Udaipur.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Teej is another Rajasthani festival dedicated to Shiva and Parvati, celebrated in the month of Shravan.

• Festivals of Rajasthan: Pushkar Camel Fair, Desert Festival (Jaisalmer), Marwar Festival (Jodhpur), Elephant Festival (Jaipur), Kite Festival.

• Mewar Festival of Udaipur also coincides with the Gangaur celebrations.

NOTE

• Folk dances of Rajasthan: Ghoomar, Kalbeliya (UNESCO Intangible Heritage, 2010), Bhavai, Chari, Kachhi Ghodi, Terah Taali.

• Rajasthan is India's largest state by area; capital Jaipur.

question: Which of the following books is authored by Indu Sundaresan?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Feast of Roses.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "The Feast of Roses" (2003) is a historical novel by the Indian-American writer Indu Sundaresan.

• It is the second book of her Taj Mahal Trilogy, which follows the life of the Mughal empress Nur Jahan (Mehrunnisa) and the court of Emperor Jahangir.

• The trilogy consists of The Twentieth Wife (2002), The Feast of Roses (2003) and Shadow Princess (2010).

• Indu Sundaresan also wrote The Splendor of Silence, In the Convent of Little Flowers and The Mountain of Light.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• "Ajaya: Rise of Kali" — written by Anand Neelakantan, who also wrote Asura: Tale of the Vanquished.

• "The Secret of the Nagas" (2011) — the second book of the Shiva Trilogy by Amish Tripathi (after *The Immortals of Meluha*, followed by *The Oath of the Vayuputras*).

• "The One You Cannot Have" — written by Preeti Shenoy.

NOTE

• Indu Sundaresan won the Washington State Book Award for *The Splendor of Silence*.

• Frequently asked author–book pairs: Jhumpa Lahiri — Interpreter of Maladies; Amitav Ghosh — The Shadow Lines, Sea of Poppies; Vikram Seth — A Suitable Boy.

question: Bhakti saints, Nayanars were devotees of which of the following gods?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shiva.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Nayanars were 63 Shaiva Bhakti saints of Tamil Nadu (roughly 6th–9th century CE) who were devotees of Lord Shiva. (नयनार — शैव संत)

• Their devotional hymns are collected in the Tevaram (and the wider Tirumurai); their lives are described in Sekkizhar's "Periyapuranam".

• The most famous Nayanars were Appar (Tirunavukkarasar), Sambandar (Tirugnana Sambandar), Sundarar and Manikkavachakar.

• Karaikkal Ammaiyar was among the few women Nayanars.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The Alvars were the 12 Vaishnava saints of Tamil Nadu, devotees of Lord Vishnu; their hymns form the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Andal was the only woman Alvar.

• Murugan (Kartikeya/Subrahmanya) is a popular Tamil deity, but the Nayanars were specifically Shiva-bhaktas.

• Indra is a Vedic deity, the god of rain and thunder — not connected with the Bhakti movement of South India.

NOTE

• Nayanars and Alvars belonged mostly to non-Brahmin and lower-caste backgrounds and preached in Tamil, opposing caste rigidity and ritualism.

• Key Bhakti saints: Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhvacharya (Dvaita), Basavanna (Lingayat/Virashaiva), Kabir, Guru Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tulsidas.

question: Hai-Hak Dance is associated with which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tripura.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Hai-Hak dance is a traditional folk dance of the Halam (Molsom) community of Tripura. (त्रिपुरा का लोक नृत्य)

• It is performed after the harvest of jhum (shifting) cultivation, in honour of the goddess of wealth Lakshmi, with the khamb (bamboo flute) and drums accompanying the dancers.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Other folk dances of Tripura: Hojagiri (Reang/Bru community — the famous balancing dance on earthen pitchers), Garia, Lebang Boomani, Bizu, Mamita, Sangrai, Wangala, Cheraw.

• Folk dances of Sikkim: Singhi Chham (snow lion dance), Maruni, Chu Faat, Yak Chham, Tamang Selo.

• Folk dances of Andhra Pradesh: Kuchipudi (classical), Vilasini Natyam, Butta Bommalu, Dhimsa, Veeranatyam, Lambadi.

• Folk dances of Rajasthan: Ghoomar, Kalbeliya, Bhavai, Chari, Kachhi Ghodi, Terah Taali, Gair.

NOTE

• Tripura — capital Agartala; it is surrounded on three sides by Bangladesh; famous sites: Ujjayanta Palace, Neermahal, Unakoti.

• India's eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam (TN), Kathak (UP), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (AP), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

question: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was founded in ________ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1928.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was founded in September 1928 at a meeting held in the ruins of Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi. (हिन्दुस्तान सोशलिस्ट रिपब्लिकन एसोसिएशन)

• It was the renamed and reorganised form of the Hindustan Republican Association (HRA), which had been set up in 1924 at Kanpur by Ramprasad Bismil, Sachindra Nath Sanyal and Jogesh Chandra Chatterjee.

• The word "Socialist" was added at the instance of Bhagat Singh, showing the shift towards a socialist republic.

• Chandrashekhar Azad was made its commander-in-chief; other members included Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra and Jatindra Nath Das.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• 1917 — Year of the Champaran Satyagraha, Gandhiji's first satyagraha in India, and of the Russian Revolution.

• 1922 — The Chauri Chaura incident (Feb 1922) led to the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

• 1924 — Founding year of the HRA at Kanpur, the parent body of the HSRA.

NOTE

• Major HSRA actions: the Saunders murder (Dec 1928, Lahore) avenging Lala Lajpat Rai's death, and the Central Legislative Assembly bomb case (8 April 1929) by Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt.

• Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged on 23 March 1931 (observed as Shaheed Diwas); Chandrashekhar Azad died at Alfred Park, Allahabad (27 February 1931).

question: Which of the following has been awarded "Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award 2021" for Wrestling?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ravi Kumar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ravi Kumar Dahiya received the Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award 2021 in the discipline of Wrestling (कुश्ती).

• He won a silver medal in the men's 57 kg freestyle wrestling event at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics (held in 2021).

• The Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award was renamed the "Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award" in August 2021; it is India's highest sporting honour.

• Major Dhyan Chand, the hockey wizard, was born on 29 August, observed as National Sports Day, on which these awards are conferred.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• A record 12 sportspersons received the Khel Ratna in 2021, including Neeraj Chopra (Athletics — Tokyo Olympics javelin gold), Sunil Chhetri (Football) and Manpreet Singh (Hockey) — but the award for Wrestling went to Ravi Kumar Dahiya.

• Other 2021 awardees: P.R. Sreejesh (Hockey), Mithali Raj (Cricket), Lovlina Borgohain (Boxing), P.V. Sindhu, Avani Lekhara, Sumit Antil, Pramod Bhagat, Krishna Nagar, Manish Narwal.

NOTE

• The Khel Ratna was instituted in 1991–92; its first recipient was chess grandmaster Viswanathan Anand.

• Sports awards hierarchy: Khel Ratna (best performance), Arjuna Award (consistent outstanding performance), Dronacharya Award (coaches), Dhyan Chand Award (lifetime achievement).

question: "PM POSHAN" Scheme is implemented by which ministry?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ministry of Education.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• PM POSHAN — Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman — is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme implemented by the Ministry of Education (Department of School Education and Literacy). (पीएम पोषण योजना)

• It was approved in September 2021, replacing the earlier Mid-Day Meal (MDM) Scheme, and provides one hot cooked meal to children in Government and Government-aided schools.

• Its coverage was extended to pre-primary (Bal Vatika) children in addition to classes I to VIII.

• The original Mid-Day Meal Scheme was launched on 15 August 1995; Tamil Nadu pioneered a mid-day meal programme much earlier under K. Kamaraj.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Ministry of Women & Child Development runs Poshan Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission, 2018), ICDS, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and Mission Shakti/Saksham Anganwadi.

• Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare runs PM-KISAN, PMFBY (crop insurance) and Kisan Credit Card.

• Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment handles welfare of SCs, OBCs, senior citizens and persons with disabilities.

NOTE

• The Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD) was renamed the Ministry of Education in July 2020 as per NEP 2020.

• Related schemes of the Ministry of Education: Samagra Shiksha, NIPUN Bharat, PM SHRI Schools, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan.

question: Which of the following is an example of an artificial ecosystem?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aquariums.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An artificial (man-made) ecosystem is one that is created and maintained by human beings, where humans control the biotic and abiotic components. (कृत्रिम पारितंत्र)

• An aquarium is the classic example — the water, temperature, light, oxygen, fish and plants are all managed by man; it is also an example of an artificial aquatic ecosystem.

• Other artificial ecosystems: crop fields, gardens/parks, orchards, dams and reservoirs, poultry farms and cities.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Grasslands — a natural terrestrial ecosystem (Prairies in North America, Steppes in Eurasia, Pampas in South America, Savanna in Africa, Velds in South Africa, Downs in Australia).

• Desert — a natural terrestrial ecosystem with very low rainfall; the Sahara is the largest hot desert, the Thar is India's largest.

• Coral reefs — a natural marine ecosystem, called the "rainforests of the sea" because of their very high biodiversity.

NOTE

• The term "ecosystem" was coined by A.G. Tansley (1935).

• Ecosystem components: biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic (light, water, air, soil, temperature); energy flow follows the 10% law of Lindeman.
